screens.title: What is AWS CodeDeploy?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodeDeploy is a managed deployment service designed to automate the release of application revisions to compute targets. In practical terms, it takes a specific revision—your code, configuration, and an AppSpec file—and ensures those files are installed consistently across the target fleet or runtime. The service removes the manual steps that often cause inconsistencies: copying files, running install scripts, starting services, and validating outcomes. CodeDeploy supports multiple compute platforms, including EC2 instances, AWS Lambda functions, Fargate tasks, and even on-premises servers, which means the same deployment model can be applied across different runtime environments. A common misconception is that CodeDeploy only copies files; in fact, the AppSpec hooks are equally important because they execute scripts at lifecycle stages to install dependencies, configure the application, and validate the service. For example, a web app revision might include a hook that installs packages in BeforeInstall, copies files in AfterInstall, and starts the web server in ApplicationStart. Understanding CodeDeploy as an orchestration layer that manages both file distribution and lifecycle scripting clarifies why it's central to reproducible deployments. Consider a case where one team member deploys manually and another automates with CodeDeploy; the automated path reduces human error and ensures each environment receives the exact same steps every time. What deployment steps in your current workflow could benefit most from this repeatability?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CodeDeploy orchestrates distribution of revisions and executes lifecycle hooks so deployments are repeatable and auditable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is AWS CodeDeploy?
Core idea
CodeDeploy automates file distribution and lifecycle hooks so deployments are deterministic.
• It accepts a revision from S3 or GitHub and installs it on targets.
• Lifecycle hooks run scripts at stages such as BeforeInstall and ValidateService.
• It supports EC2, Lambda, Fargate, and on-premises targets, enabling consistent flows.
Analogy: Deployment as a Scripted Recipe
Think of CodeDeploy as a kitchen where the recipe is the AppSpec file and the revision is the set of ingredients. The agent follows the recipe steps on every target so each server serves the same dish.
Example
A static site revision provides index.html and a script. AppSpec hooks install the web server, copy files, and start the service. CodeDeploy reports events for each hook so you can see success or failure per step.
Key Takeaway

CodeDeploy enforces a repeatable, scripted deployment process across diverse compute targets, reducing manual error.

screens.title: CodeDeploy architecture & components
screens.narratorSegment: CodeDeploy's architecture is purposefully simple, built from four main pieces that together enable automated deployments. First, an Application represents the logical software artifact you want to release — a web app, A P I, or microservice. Within an Application you create Deployment Groups. Each Deployment Group targets a set of compute resources, defined by EC2 tags, Auto Scaling groups, or Lambda function identifiers, and it also contains the deployment settings such as the deployment type and a service role. The Revision is the actual bundle: your code, configuration files, and the AppSpec file. Revisions are stored in S3 or in a GitHub repository, and a specific revision is what you point to when you start a deployment. The CodeDeploy Agent runs on EC2 or on-premises hosts; this agent polls for deployment instructions, downloads the revision, and executes the AppSpec lifecycle hooks. A common mistake is assuming the agent will magically find scripts — the AppSpec file must include correct relative paths and the scripts must be executable on the host. For example, if your AppSpec lists scripts/install_dependencies. sh, that path must exist in the root of the revision and the agent will run it during BeforeInstall. Understanding these components helps you design deployment groups that match environments such as dev, staging, and prod, and it clarifies why permissions, tags, and file locations are critical.

keyIdea.title: Component mapping
keyIdea.text: Application groups revisions and deployment groups; agent executes the AppSpec on each target to enact the revision.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Components
Component roles
Application
Logical container for deployment groups and revisions.
Deployment Group
Defines targets, deployment type, and the service role for actions.
Revision
The zipped bundle in S3 or GitHub with code, config, and AppSpec.
CodeDeploy Agent
Runs on hosts, downloads revisions, and executes lifecycle hooks locally.
Common misconception
Some assume the service alone performs installs; actually, the agent executes scripts on the host. If the agent is not running or scripts are missing, the deployment will fail.
Concrete example
For a web app: Application = MyWebApp, Deployment Group = MyWebApp-Dev targeting EC2 instances with Name tag 'dev', Revision = my-web-app.zip in S3, Agent = running on each EC2 instance pulling the revision and running install/start scripts.
Key Takeaway

Map each component to your release process so roles and permissions are clear before you deploy.

screens.title: In-place vs Blue/Green deployments
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between in-place and blue/green deployments depends on your tolerance for downtime, rollback needs, and infrastructure constraints. In-place deployments update the application directly on each instance: CodeDeploy stops the app, installs the new revision, restarts the app, and validates the service. The advantage is simplicity and lower resource usage because you reuse existing instances. But in-place can cause brief downtime or a temporary reduction in capacity, especially when many instances update at once or when a script fails mid-process. Blue/green deployments aim for zero downtime by provisioning a separate green environment that runs the new revision alongside the stable blue environment. Once the green environment is validated, traffic shifts from blue to green. This makes rollback trivial: you can shift traffic back to blue if something goes wrong. The trade-off is additional cost and orchestration complexity: you must provision new instances, configure load balancers or routing, and ensure the green environment mirrors production configuration. A common misconception is that blue/green always eliminates risk; while it minimizes user impact, you still must validate the green environment fully and ensure database and shared-state migrations are safe. For critical production applications where uptime and quick rollback are essential, blue/green is preferred. For small updates or constrained environments, in-place with cautious deployment configuration can be acceptable.

keyIdea.text: In-place is simpler and cost-efficient; blue/green reduces user impact and speeds rollback but requires extra resources and validation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › In-place vs Blue/Green
In-place deployments
Updates occur on the existing instances. Use deployment configurations to control parallelism.
  • Pros: simpler, cost-efficient.
  • Cons: potential brief downtime, harder rollback.
  • Use when you can tolerate short interruptions or have small fleets.
Blue/Green deployments
Provision a new environment, validate it, then shift traffic. Ideal for zero-downtime releases.
  • Pros: minimal user impact, easy rollback.
  • Cons: higher resource usage, more orchestration.
  • Use for critical production systems requiring high availability.
Decision tip

Choose blue/green when user-facing uptime and rollback speed outweigh the cost of extra instances. Use in-place for lower-cost environments with controlled update windows.

screens.title: AppSpec file: structure and purpose
screens.narratorSegment: The AppSpec file is the heart of a CodeDeploy revision. It’s a YAML file placed at the root of your application bundle that tells CodeDeploy which files to copy, where to put them, and which lifecycle event scripts to run. For EC2 and on-premises deployments you declare a version and OS, list files with source and destination paths, and define hooks such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, and ValidateService. Each hook can list multiple scripts with an optional timeout and run-as user. The key operational rules are simple but critical: paths in files and hooks are relative to the root of the revision bundle, scripts must be present and executable, and timeouts should be generous enough for operations like package installation. A frequent error is incorrect script paths leading to failures during a lifecycle event; another is forgetting to make scripts executable before zipping the bundle. Below is a concise example appspec. yml used in EC2 in-place deployments. Inspect it and note how files and hooks map to concrete actions during deployment. AppSpec file: structure and purpose means appspec maps files and hooks; correct relative paths and executable permissions are essential to successful deployments.. In practical terms, a yaml blueprint that instructs codedeploy how to install and validate a revision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AppSpec essentials
keyIdea.text: AppSpec maps files and hooks; correct relative paths and executable permissions are essential to successful deployments.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › AppSpec Structure
What AppSpec declares
  • Files to copy from the revision and their destination paths on the instance.
  • Lifecycle event hooks and the scripts to execute at each stage.
  • Timeouts and the user identity used to run scripts.
Remember: locations are relative to the root of the zipped revision. If a script is missing or not executable, the corresponding lifecycle event will fail and you’ll need to check agent logs to diagnose it.
Example appspec.yml
version: 0.0
os: linux
files:
  - source: /index.html
    destination: /var/www/html/
  - source: /scripts/start_server.sh
    destination: /tmp/
hooks:
  BeforeInstall:
    - location: scripts/install_dependencies.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  AfterInstall:
    - location: scripts/configure_application.sh
      timeout: 300
      runas: root
  ApplicationStart:
    - location: scripts/start_server.sh
      timeout: 60
      runas: root
  ValidateService:
    - location: scripts/validate_service.sh
      timeout: 60
      runas: root
This example copies files, runs dependency install, configures the app, starts the server, and runs a validation script. Ensure paths exist in the revision and scripts are executable.

screens.title: Prepare application bundle and scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Preparing a revision bundle requires a predictable directory layout and small executable scripts for lifecycle hooks. In the hands-on example we create a my-web-app directory with index. html at the root, an appspec. yml file also at the root, and a scripts directory containing install and start scripts. The index. html is the asset that will be served by the web server; the appspec. yml lists where to copy it and which scripts to run. Scripts should begin with a proper shell shebang and be given execute permissions before zipping. A common mistake is zipping files from a parent directory which results in an extra top-level folder inside the zip; the agent then cannot find files at the expected relative paths. Another pitfall is forgetting sudo where needed or not enabling a service. Below are the concrete files used in the chapter lab. When you create these files locally, run chmod +x on the scripts, then zip the directory so the appspec remains at the bundle root. This step ensures CodeDeploy can find files and run hooks exactly as declared.

keyIdea.text: Maintain a flat root containing appspec.yml and files referenced by it; make scripts executable and zip at the correct level.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Prepare bundle
Folder layout
Keep appspec.yml at the bundle root. Put scripts in a scripts/ directory and assets at the root or nested as declared.
  • Ensure scripts include a shebang (#!/bin/bash) and are executable.
  • Zip the directory so appspec.yml is directly inside the zip root, not within an extra parent folder.
  • Validate by unzipping locally and checking relative paths before uploading.
Example files
index.html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>My CodeDeploy App</title>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Hello from CodeDeploy!</h1>
    <p>This page was deployed using AWS CodeDeploy.</p>
</body>
</html>
install_httpd.sh and start_httpd.sh should include package installation and service enable commands. Make them executable before packaging.

screens.title: Install the CodeDeploy agent on EC2
screens.narratorSegment: The CodeDeploy agent is the runtime daemon that executes the deployment instructions on each EC2 or on-premises host. Installing and verifying the agent is an essential step before creating a deployment group. On Amazon Linux 2, you typically update packages, install ruby and wget, download the agent installer from the region-specific S3 location, make it executable, and run the install script. After installation, verify the agent service status. If the agent is not running, it cannot receive deployment instructions and the deployment will not proceed. Another common issue is missing the agent in instances launched via Auto Scaling; include the agent installation in user-data to ensure new instances start with the agent already installed. The commands below are the sequence used in the lab; adjust the wget URL for your region if required. If installation appears to succeed but deployments still fail, check the agent logs for startup errors and the instance IAM instance profile to ensure the agent can access S3 for revisions. Install the CodeDeploy agent on EC2 means the codedeploy agent executes appspec hooks locally; ensure it is installed, running, and included in instance user data for auto scaling.. Install & verify
Run the installer and confirm the agent is active. For Auto Scaling, include the commands in user-data so new instances are ready.
If the agent service fails to start, check /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/codedeploy-agent.log for startup errors and ensure required packages like ruby are available.
Example install commands

sudo yum install -y ruby
sudo yum install -y wget
cd /home/ec2-user

screens.title: Diagnose deployment failures
screens.narratorSegment: When a deployment fails, the CodeDeploy console Event view provides a quick high-level pointer, but real diagnosis requires the CodeDeploy agent logs on the target instance. Inspect /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/codedeploy-agent. log for agent lifecycle messages and then review the deployment-specific logs under /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/deployment-logs. Those logs capture stdout and stderr for each lifecycle script, showing package install errors, missing files, or permission denials. Common failure causes include incorrect AppSpec paths, non-executable scripts, missing dependencies during install scripts, and IAM or S3 permission issues preventing the agent from downloading the revision. For example, an AfterInstall script may fail because a package manager command returned an error; the deployment log will show the exact command output and error code. Another typical scenario is forgetting to give the instance an instance profile that grants S3 read access; then the agent cannot download the bundle. The troubleshooting flow is: check Events for the failed lifecycle stage, SSH into the instance, open the agent logs and the deployment-specific logs, and correct the script or permission problem before retrying. This systematic approach prevents guesswork and speeds recovery. Diagnose deployment failures means check events, ssh to instance, inspect agent logs and deployment logs to identify the failing hook and fix scripts or permissions.. In practical terms, use codedeploy events and agent logs to find script and permission errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Troubleshoot
Diagnosis flow
  1. Open the CodeDeploy console Events and find the failed lifecycle event.
  2. SSH into the target EC2 instance and check /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/codedeploy-agent.log.
  3. Open deployment logs under /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/deployment-logs/ to view stdout/stderr from scripts.
  4. Fix the failing script, permissions, or instance role and retry the deployment.
Example log excerpt
[ERROR] /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/XYZ/scripts/install_dependencies.sh: line 12: yum: command not found Script failed with exit code 127
This shows a missing package manager binary or PATH issue. The log pinpoints the script and the failing command so you can correct the script or environment.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore how AWS CodeDeploy automates application releases so they are consistent and safe. You will learn the core components — Application, Deployment Group, and Revision — and see when to choose in-place updates versus blue/green strategies for zero-downtime releases. We'll also unpack the AppSpec file, the single source of instructions that CodeDeploy uses to copy files and run lifecycle hooks on targets. Practically, you will follow a hands-on flow to prepare an application bundle with an AppSpec and simple shell scripts, install the CodeDeploy agent on an EC2 instance, upload your revision to S3, and start a deployment. Along the way, I’ll show common pitfalls, how to diagnose failures with agent logs, and why lifecycle hooks need correct paths and executable permissions. By the end, you’ll understand how CodeDeploy enforces repeatability and how it reduces manual error during releases. Think about a recent manual release you performed — imagine replacing those checklists with a repeatable revision and AppSpec so each deployment behaves the same way.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify CodeDeploy’s core components, choose an appropriate deployment strategy, author an AppSpec file, configure a deployment group, and diagnose failures. First, you will learn to map Application, Deployment Group, and Revision to your release workflow so deployments are repeatable. Next, you will compare in-place versus blue/green strategies with real trade-offs — when zero downtime matters and when a simple in-place update suffices. You will author an AppSpec for EC2-style deployments, listing files and lifecycle hooks, and learn common mistakes like wrong file paths or non-executable scripts. You will also set up the CodeDeploy agent and the IAM service role needed to grant CodeDeploy permissions. Finally, you will practice analyzing agent logs and CodeDeploy events to find script errors and permission issues. Throughout, we’ll ground objectives with a short hands-on example: packaging a small web page, uploading it to S3, and running an in-place deployment to an EC2 instance so you understand each step and its purpose.

You will practice a sequence of practical tasks designed to cement each objective. Start by creating an IAM service role for CodeDeploy so the service can access S3 and interact with EC2; this teaches the principle of least privilege and the role that service permissions play in deployments. Then prepare a small application bundle with index. html, an AppSpec file, and two shell scripts to install and start a web server. You will zip the bundle and upload it to S3 to become a Revision. Next you will install and verify the CodeDeploy agent on a target EC2 instance; learning how the agent pulls the revision and runs hooks clarifies where deployment failures usually occur. Finally, you will create an application and deployment group, run an in-place deployment, and practice checking the CodeDeploy console and agent logs when something fails. Each task is short but exacting: file paths, script permissions, and the correct AppSpec locations must be right. These practices mirror production workflows and build troubleshooting skills you will use daily.

AWS CodeDeploy is a managed deployment service designed to automate the release of application revisions to compute targets. In practical terms, it takes a specific revision—your code, configuration, and an AppSpec file—and ensures those files are installed consistently across the target fleet or runtime. The service removes the manual steps that often cause inconsistencies: copying files, running install scripts, starting services, and validating outcomes. CodeDeploy supports multiple compute platforms, including EC2 instances, AWS Lambda functions, Fargate tasks, and even on-premises servers, which means the same deployment model can be applied across different runtime environments. A common misconception is that CodeDeploy only copies files; in fact, the AppSpec hooks are equally important because they execute scripts at lifecycle stages to install dependencies, configure the application, and validate the service. For example, a web app revision might include a hook that installs packages in BeforeInstall, copies files in AfterInstall, and starts the web server in ApplicationStart. Understanding CodeDeploy as an orchestration layer that manages both file distribution and lifecycle scripting clarifies why it's central to reproducible deployments. Consider a case where one team member deploys manually and another automates with CodeDeploy; the automated path reduces human error and ensures each environment receives the exact same steps every time. What deployment steps in your current workflow could benefit most from this repeatability?

CodeDeploy's architecture is purposefully simple, built from four main pieces that together enable automated deployments. First, an Application represents the logical software artifact you want to release — a web app, A P I, or microservice. Within an Application you create Deployment Groups. Each Deployment Group targets a set of compute resources, defined by EC2 tags, Auto Scaling groups, or Lambda function identifiers, and it also contains the deployment settings such as the deployment type and a service role. The Revision is the actual bundle: your code, configuration files, and the AppSpec file. Revisions are stored in S3 or in a GitHub repository, and a specific revision is what you point to when you start a deployment. The CodeDeploy Agent runs on EC2 or on-premises hosts; this agent polls for deployment instructions, downloads the revision, and executes the AppSpec lifecycle hooks. A common mistake is assuming the agent will magically find scripts — the AppSpec file must include correct relative paths and the scripts must be executable on the host. For example, if your AppSpec lists scripts/install_dependencies. sh, that path must exist in the root of the revision and the agent will run it during BeforeInstall. Understanding these components helps you design deployment groups that match environments such as dev, staging, and prod, and it clarifies why permissions, tags, and file locations are critical.

Choosing between in-place and blue/green deployments depends on your tolerance for downtime, rollback needs, and infrastructure constraints. In-place deployments update the application directly on each instance: CodeDeploy stops the app, installs the new revision, restarts the app, and validates the service. The advantage is simplicity and lower resource usage because you reuse existing instances. But in-place can cause brief downtime or a temporary reduction in capacity, especially when many instances update at once or when a script fails mid-process. Blue/green deployments aim for zero downtime by provisioning a separate green environment that runs the new revision alongside the stable blue environment. Once the green environment is validated, traffic shifts from blue to green. This makes rollback trivial: you can shift traffic back to blue if something goes wrong. The trade-off is additional cost and orchestration complexity: you must provision new instances, configure load balancers or routing, and ensure the green environment mirrors production configuration. A common misconception is that blue/green always eliminates risk; while it minimizes user impact, you still must validate the green environment fully and ensure database and shared-state migrations are safe. For critical production applications where uptime and quick rollback are essential, blue/green is preferred. For small updates or constrained environments, in-place with cautious deployment configuration can be acceptable.

The AppSpec file is the heart of a CodeDeploy revision. It’s a YAML file placed at the root of your application bundle that tells CodeDeploy which files to copy, where to put them, and which lifecycle event scripts to run. For EC2 and on-premises deployments you declare a version and OS, list files with source and destination paths, and define hooks such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart, and ValidateService. Each hook can list multiple scripts with an optional timeout and run-as user. The key operational rules are simple but critical: paths in files and hooks are relative to the root of the revision bundle, scripts must be present and executable, and timeouts should be generous enough for operations like package installation. A frequent error is incorrect script paths leading to failures during a lifecycle event; another is forgetting to make scripts executable before zipping the bundle. Below is a concise example appspec. yml used in EC2 in-place deployments. Inspect it and note how files and hooks map to concrete actions during deployment. AppSpec file: structure and purpose means appspec maps files and hooks; correct relative paths and executable permissions are essential to successful deployments.. In practical terms, a yaml blueprint that instructs codedeploy how to install and validate a revision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Preparing a revision bundle requires a predictable directory layout and small executable scripts for lifecycle hooks. In the hands-on example we create a my-web-app directory with index. html at the root, an appspec. yml file also at the root, and a scripts directory containing install and start scripts. The index. html is the asset that will be served by the web server; the appspec. yml lists where to copy it and which scripts to run. Scripts should begin with a proper shell shebang and be given execute permissions before zipping. A common mistake is zipping files from a parent directory which results in an extra top-level folder inside the zip; the agent then cannot find files at the expected relative paths. Another pitfall is forgetting sudo where needed or not enabling a service. Below are the concrete files used in the chapter lab. When you create these files locally, run chmod +x on the scripts, then zip the directory so the appspec remains at the bundle root. This step ensures CodeDeploy can find files and run hooks exactly as declared.

The CodeDeploy agent is the runtime daemon that executes the deployment instructions on each EC2 or on-premises host. Installing and verifying the agent is an essential step before creating a deployment group. On Amazon Linux 2, you typically update packages, install ruby and wget, download the agent installer from the region-specific S3 location, make it executable, and run the install script. After installation, verify the agent service status. If the agent is not running, it cannot receive deployment instructions and the deployment will not proceed. Another common issue is missing the agent in instances launched via Auto Scaling; include the agent installation in user-data to ensure new instances start with the agent already installed. The commands below are the sequence used in the lab; adjust the wget URL for your region if required. If installation appears to succeed but deployments still fail, check the agent logs for startup errors and the instance IAM instance profile to ensure the agent can access S3 for revisions. Install the CodeDeploy agent on EC2 means the codedeploy agent executes appspec hooks locally; ensure it is installed, running, and included in instance user data for auto scaling.. In practical terms, agent must run on targets to download revisions and run hooks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating a CodeDeploy Application and a Deployment Group binds your revision to targets and a deployment configuration. Start by creating an IAM service role for CodeDeploy, granting it permissions to interact with EC2, S3, and other services. When you create the deployment group, specify whether it targets EC2 instances by tag, an Auto Scaling group, or Lambda functions. Select the deployment type: in-place or blue/green, and pick a deployment configuration such as CodeDeployDefault. OneAtATime to control parallelism. For the service role, attach the CodeDeploy service role you created so CodeDeploy can act on resources on your behalf. When a deployment fails, the CodeDeploy console Event view provides a quick high-level pointer, but real diagnosis requires the CodeDeploy agent logs on the target instance. Inspect /var/log/aws/codedeploy-agent/codedeploy-agent. log for agent lifecycle messages and then review the deployment-specific logs under /opt/codedeploy-agent/deployment-root/deployment-logs. Those logs capture stdout and stderr for each lifecycle script, showing package install errors, missing files, or permission denials. Common failure causes include incorrect AppSpec paths, non-executable scripts, missing dependencies during install scripts, and IAM or S3 permission issues preventing the agent from downloading the revision. For example, an AfterInstall script may fail because a package manager command returned an error; the deployment log will show the exact command output and error code. Another typical scenario is forgetting to give the instance an instance profile that grants S3 read access; then the agent cannot download the bundle. The troubleshooting flow is: check Events for the failed lifecycle stage, SSH into the instance, open the agent logs and the deployment-specific logs, and correct the script or permission problem before retrying.
